lead: Memory holds the program and data that the CPU uses. It is built as a hierarchy: small, fast, costly storage near the CPU and large, slow, cheap storage far away. Memory organization connects this hierarchy to the address bus: n address lines give 2ⁿ locations, and decoders place ROM and RAM chips at fixed ranges called the memory map. You use these ideas when you write a memory map for an 8085 or 8086 board, or when you read the separate program and data spaces of an 8051.
prereq: You need: Chapter 1.2 for address, data and control buses, and Chapter 1.3 for the stored-program idea; basic powers of 2 from school maths.

sections.h3: Bits, bytes, words and the hierarchy

blocks.text: A bit is one binary digit, 0 or 1. A byte is 8 bits. A word is the group of bits the CPU handles in one operation; it may be 8, 16, 32 or 64 bits. An address is a number that names one storage location. Capacity is the number of locations times the bits in each location, usually quoted in bytes. Volatile memory loses its contents when power is removed. Non-volatile memory keeps them.

RAM is read-write and volatile. SRAM stores each bit in a flip-flop, needs no refresh, is fast, and uses more area and power per bit. DRAM stores each bit as charge on a capacitor, needs periodic refresh, is denser and cheaper, and is slower. Cache is small SRAM close to the CPU. Main memory is DRAM. Secondary storage is flash, SSD, hard disk or tape.

ROM is read-only in normal use. Mask ROM is fixed at manufacture. PROM is programmed once by the user. EPROM is erased with ultraviolet light and reprogrammed. EEPROM is erased electrically, byte by byte or in blocks. Flash is an EEPROM variant erased in blocks; it holds firmware and SSD data. The hierarchy from registers to cache to main memory to flash to disk trades speed for size and cost per bit.

n address lines select 2ⁿ locations. For 16 lines, 2¹⁶ = 65536 locations. If each location is one byte, the address space is 65536 bytes = 64 KB, from 0000H to FFFFH. Byte-addressable memory gives every byte its own address. Word-addressable memory gives one address to a whole word, so consecutive addresses differ by one word, not one byte.

blocks.where: n is the number of address lines; w is the number of bytes per location; w = 1 for byte-addressable memory.

blocks.text: Address decoding turns an address into a chip select. The CPU drives the address bus. A decoder checks the high-order bits. Its output selects exactly one ROM or RAM chip. The low-order bits choose the location inside that chip. A memory map is the list of address ranges given to ROM, RAM and I/O. Read-only regions hold code, tables and constants. Read-write regions hold variables, stack and heap.

Use capacity to find a range. A chip of C bytes starting at S ends at S + C − 1. On a 16-bit map, an 8 KB ROM has 8192 bytes = 2000H, so it occupies 2000H addresses. A 2 KB RAM has 2048 bytes = 0800H. Check that ranges do not overlap.

sections.h3: The memory map, the stack and separate spaces

blocks.text: A CPU sees memory as a map, not as separate chips. A common layout puts ROM at low addresses for reset code and fixed constants, and RAM at higher addresses for variables, stack and heap. The stack is a read-write RAM area that grows and shrinks. The stack pointer holds the address of the current top. Calls and interrupts push return addresses and saved registers; returns pop them. The stack is therefore ordinary RAM plus a pointer, not a separate memory type. Detailed push and pop instructions are in Unit 3.

Some microcontrollers have separate program and data address spaces. The 8051 is an example: code fetches use program memory, data uses data memory. This is a Harvard arrangement; one shared space is von Neumann (Chapter 1.3). The 8051 internal details and special function registers belong to Unit 4.
A wrong chip select can place two chips at the same address. The bus then drives conflicting data and the program fails. Always write the memory map and check every range.

figure.caption: The stack runs from registers at the top to disk or tape at the bottom. Moving down gives more capacity but longer access time and lower cost per bit.

spec.aria: A memory hierarchy stack runs from registers at the top through cache, main memory and flash to hard disk or tape at the bottom, getting slower and larger.

examples.question: A byte-addressable memory has 16 address lines. An 8 KB ROM is placed at 0000H and a 2 KB RAM at 2000H. Find the address range of the ROM and the RAM, and the total address space.
steps: n = 16, so total address space = 2¹⁶ = 65536 bytes = 64 KB. The highest address is FFFFH.
ROM size = 8 × 1024 = 8192 bytes = 2000H. Last offset inside the ROM = 8192 − 1 = 8191 = 1FFFH.
ROM starts at 0000H, so ROM ends at 0000H + 1FFFH = 1FFFH. ROM range = 0000H to 1FFFH.
RAM size = 2 × 1024 = 2048 bytes = 0800H. Last offset inside the RAM = 2048 − 1 = 2047 = 07FFH.
RAM starts at 2000H, so RAM ends at 2000H + 07FFH = 27FFH. RAM range = 2000H to 27FFH.
The RAM end 27FFH is 10239 in decimal.
Used memory = 8192 + 2048 = 10240 bytes = 10 KB. Free memory = 65536 − 10240 = 55296 bytes = 54 KB.
examples.answer: ROM: 0000H–1FFFH (8192 bytes); RAM: 2000H–27FFH (2048 bytes); total address space: 65536 bytes.
examples.check:
n = 16
rom_kb = 8
ram_kb = 2
rom_start = 0x0000
ram_start = 0x2000

rom_size = rom_kb * 1024
ram_size = ram_kb * 1024
total = 2 ** n

rom_offset_last = rom_size - 1
ram_offset_last = ram_size - 1
ram_end = ram_start + ram_offset_last
used = rom_size + ram_size
free = total - used

for value in [total, rom_size, ram_size, rom_offset_last, ram_offset_last, ram_end, used, free]:
    print(value)

traps: End address is start + size − 1. Adding the full size gives the first address after the region, not the last address inside it.
1 K = 1024, so 8 KB = 8192 bytes = 2000H, not 8000 bytes. A 2 KB chip is 0800H bytes, not 0200H.
Byte-addressable and word-addressable are not the same: 65536 addresses cover 64 KB of bytes or 128 KB of 16-bit words.
SRAM is a RAM, not a ROM. SRAM is fast and volatile; flash is non-volatile but writable in blocks, not read-only forever.
Chip select enables a whole chip; the low address bits choose the location inside. Do not call a chip-select line an address line.

quiz.q: Define bit, byte and word. Give the number of bits in each.
quiz.a: A bit is one binary digit, 0 or 1. A byte is 8 bits. A word is the CPU's natural group of bits; its size may be 8, 16, 32 or 64 bits depending on the CPU.

quiz.q: Why does the memory hierarchy put SRAM cache between the CPU and DRAM main memory?
quiz.a: SRAM is faster than DRAM but smaller and costlier per bit. A small SRAM cache holds recently used blocks, so many CPU requests are served quickly without waiting for DRAM.

quiz.q: A byte-addressable memory has 12 address lines. Find the total address space and the range of a 1 KB ROM placed at 000H.
quiz.a: Total address space = 2¹² = 4096 bytes = 4 KB. 1 KB = 1024 bytes = 400H. Last offset = 1024 − 1 = 1023 = 3FFH. ROM range = 000H to 3FFH.

quiz.q: A 16-bit byte-addressable map has ROM 0000H–1FFFH and RAM 2000H–27FFH. A student places a 1 KB RAM chip at 2800H. Does it overlap the existing RAM? Find its end and the free space after it.
quiz.a: 1 KB = 1024 bytes = 400H. The new RAM ends at 2800H + 3FFH = 2BFFH. It starts at 2800H, just after 27FFH, so it does not overlap. Free space after it = FFFFH − 2BFFH = D400H = 54272 bytes = 53 KB.

quiz.q: Name two differences between SRAM and DRAM.
quiz.a: SRAM stores a bit in a flip-flop and needs no refresh; DRAM stores charge on a capacitor and needs refresh. SRAM is faster and costlier per bit; DRAM is denser and cheaper per bit.

quiz.q: Why is flash called non-volatile but not ROM in the strict sense?
quiz.a: Flash keeps its data when power is removed, so it is non-volatile. It can be erased and rewritten electrically in blocks, so it is read-write in normal use, unlike mask ROM which is fixed at manufacture.

quiz.q: How many address lines are needed for a 32 KB byte-addressable memory?
quiz.a: 32 KB = 32 × 1024 = 32768 bytes = 2¹⁵. Therefore 15 address lines are needed.

beyond: Not for the exam. Industry memory is a stack of DDR5 DRAM, HBM for GPUs, 3D NAND flash and on-chip SRAM caches; memory controllers schedule refresh and bank access. Research explores persistent memory, compute-in-memory and cache coherence. Search for "DDR SDRAM timing", "NAND flash pages and blocks" and "memory map of a microcontroller".
